reference.source: Comprehensive Clinical Nephrology / Brenner and Rector's The Kidney
clinicalPearls: The commonest cause of acute kidney injury in multiple myeloma, driven by high circulating free light chains
Filtered monoclonal free light chains bind Tamm-Horsfall protein and precipitate as obstructing casts in the distal tubules
Biopsy shows dense, fractured, angulated tubular casts surrounded by a cellular reaction, often with giant cells and tubular injury
Presentation is typically acute or subacute kidney injury, sometimes precipitated by dehydration, hypercalcaemia, infection, contrast or nephrotoxic drugs
Urine dipstick underestimates the proteinuria because it detects albumin rather than the predominant light-chain (Bence Jones) protein
Diagnosis rests on serum free light-chain assay, serum and urine electrophoresis with immunofixation, and confirmation of the plasma-cell clone
Management combines rapid reduction of the pathogenic light chain by clone-directed therapy for the paraprotein-related disease with correction of precipitating factors and supportive care
reference.pathophysiology: In multiple myeloma a plasma-cell clone secretes large amounts of monoclonal free light chains that are filtered by the glomerulus and delivered to the distal nephron. There they co-aggregate with Tamm-Horsfall (uromodulin) protein secreted by the thick ascending limb, forming dense, waxy, often fractured casts that obstruct tubular flow and incite an inflammatory and giant-cell reaction with tubular epithelial injury. Obstruction and back-pressure reduce glomerular filtration, producing acute kidney injury, while direct proximal tubular toxicity of light chains adds further damage. Volume depletion, hypercalcaemia, loop diuretics, contrast and nephrotoxins promote cast formation by concentrating light chains and reducing flow, explaining common precipitants.
additionalDifferentials: Acute tubular injury from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Serum free light-chain assay with the kappa-to-lambda ratio
Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation
Bone marrow examination to confirm the plasma-cell clone
Serum calcium, renal function and full blood count
Renal biopsy where the diagnosis or reversibility is uncertain
Imaging for lytic bone lesions and assessment of infection or dehydration
redFlags: Severe or dialysis-requiring acute kidney injury
reference.prognosis: Renal recovery depends on the speed and depth of light-chain reduction and on the degree of established tubular and interstitial damage at diagnosis; early, effective clone-directed therapy offers the best chance of renal recovery and improved survival. Extensive cast formation with fibrosis and a delayed light-chain response predict dialysis dependence.
pitfalls: Relying on urine dipstick, which misses Bence Jones proteinuria
Missing precipitants such as dehydration, hypercalcaemia, contrast and loop diuretics
Delaying clone-directed therapy while awaiting biopsy in clear-cut cases
Confusing cast nephropathy with light chain deposition disease or amyloidosis
Giving nephrotoxic drugs that worsen cast formation
management: Start clone-directed anti-myeloma therapy urgently, typically a bortezomib-based regimen with dexamethasone, to reduce circulating free light chains rapidly
Correct volume depletion with intravenous fluids to increase distal tubular flow and dilute light chains, limiting cast formation
Treat coexisting hypercalcaemia with hydration and a bisphosphonate
Withdraw nephrotoxins and avoid iodinated contrast, loop diuretics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs that promote cast precipitation
Provide renal replacement therapy for refractory acute kidney injury and uraemic complications
Monitor serum free light chains and renal function to gauge depth of response and prospects for renal recovery
Manage jointly with haematology and nephrology, and consider renal biopsy where the diagnosis or reversibility is uncertain
